messages.subject: 2D digitisation horse's feet
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm afraid I'm next to Geomorph so my questions are quite basic:
My project involves measuring lengths/angles/ratios between various landmarks on photographs of (live) horse's feet, which seems to be different from what most other people use this for but presumably it should still work?
I have tried to follow instructions on importing photos and digitising them in 2D but just get a load of error images (see below). I was wondering if anyone has any example code that I could use to get started, or recommendations of tutorials?
We are taking photographs from the front, the side and underneath the hoof, is is possible to use these views to create 3D images using Geomorph?

Thanks in advance,

Sarah

messages.subject: trajectory analysis with "non-independent" population pairs
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a couple of geomorph-specific (but probably also more statistical/conceptual) questions regarding measuring the extent of parallel phenotypic evolution.

Briefly, I have data for eight fish populations. Two of those are from very large lakes (let's call them Source1 and Source2), which have acted as source for the other six small populations (Derived1 - Derived6).
One of the small lakes (Derived1) has been colonized from Source1, whereas the other five (Derived2 - 6) have been colonized from Source2.

My main aim is to quantify the extent (amount and direction) of phenotypic change of all small lake populations, but I ran into some problems given the "non-independence" of my population pairs.

First, I was thinking about analyzing this using the trajectory.analysis function, but my data does not seem to fit the generic input data format as one and the same population (Source2) would have to be assigned to several pairs (unless I missed something obvious).
I can get the function running by duplicating individuals from Source2 several times and assigning them to five "independent" pairs. The output seems to make sense, but I am not sure about the effects of this. A plot of the first two axes of a PCA with and without the duplicated individuals (independent GPAs) looks almost identical and the PC axes explain an almost identical amount of variation. Thus, I am tempted to conclude that duplicating these individuals did not have a strong effect and given some caveats I can use this approach. Yet, I am wondering what people with more experience and a stronger statistical background think. Is this procedure justifiable?

I also performed all five possible independent analyses (Source1Derived1 / Source2Derived2, Source1Derived1 / Source2Derived3, etc.), but since the results are then derived from independent GPAs and PCAs I assume I cannot properly compare the five small lakes (e.g. even qualitatively saying Source2Derived2 is parallel to Source1Derived1, so if Source2Derived3 is not parallel to Source1Derived1, then Source2Derived2 and Source2Derived3 don't show a lot parallelism ). Is that correct? One cannot compare trajectories from independent analyses (even though one population pair is always the same).

Alternatively, I thought about using advanced.procD.lm similar to what has been described in a recent post here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/trajectory%7Csort:relevance/geomorph-r-package/wbxkMp35W6o/2kyMKw5BAQAJ>, however I would be interested in the difference in lengths and angles among all pairs and I am not sure how to do this (get the angles). Also, is there a convenient way to plot the vectors in 2D-space (analogous to a plot of the TA)?

Any comments or suggestions on my thoughts and how I should proceed would be very much appreciated.

Thanks,
Andi

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] trajectory analysis with "non-independent" population pairs
messages.body_plain:
Andy,

I think the best way to go about this is a two-pronged approach.  Your instincts for trajectory analysis were good, but as you have found out, that is a function for a factorial model.  But yes, you can do something similar with advanced.procD.lm.

First prong, I would use procD.lm to see if pairwise tests are warranted.

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ derived/source, …)

This will have to be updated for nested effects.

fit <- update.nested(fit, ~derived/source)
summary(fit)

If the derived effect is not significant, you can stop here.  If significant, I think this should work as the second prong:

fit2 <- advanced.procD.lm(Y ~ derived/source, ~ source, groups = ~derived, ...)

summary(fit2)

This approach assumes - as you have suggested - that the original sources 1 and 2 are levels represented in your variable, derived.  The approach above will allow you to test if the vectors between least squares means are significantly longer than expected by chance, holding constant the variation between source populations.  Thus, any source-derived value that is significant means the new populations have significantly diverged in terms of the magnitude of phenotypic change.  You could also create vectors of phenotypic change like in the post you linked.  Either way should work.

To ascertain if the derived populations changed in different directions is a bit trickier.  You would have to create the vectors like in the post you linked, but calculate either the vector correlation or angle between vectors for every random permutation.  We currently do not have all the random means as output, just because it normally would be cumbersome.  We could update that, and then you would have to figure out how to calculate all vector correlations or angles between different vectors, in every permutation.  Just as easily (relatively speaking), one could write a routine that does advanced.procD.lm with 1 iteration many times in a (randomization) loop and extract the LS means each time.  Regardless, the intent here is to recreate what trajectory analysis does, when one does not have a factorial model.

Finally, one bit of output from advanced.procD.lm is the LS means.  Save these and do a PCA; e.g.,

myMeans <- fit2$LS.means
PCA <- prcomp(myMeans)
P <- Y%*%PCA$rotation # project data onto between-group PC axes
Pm <- myMeans%*%PCA$rotation # project means onto between-group PC axes
plot(P[,1:2], cex=0.5, …) # plot rotated data space, add color to points if desired
points(Pm[,1:2], cex=1.5, …) # add big points for means; now you have something similar to trajectory plot

If you do not do the direction test, this plot might help inform if the direction of phenotypic change was consistent.

Hope this was helpful!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Mike,

Thank you so much for your fast and very elaborate reply! That was really helpful.

I'm afraid I still have some questions, though.

1.) I am a bit confused about the variables in your example. You wrote that "...the original sources 1 and 2 are levels represented in your variable, derived". So, in your example "derived" would only have two levels (Source1 and Source2) and "source" would specify the individual lakes. Is that correct? Sorry, just regarding the variable names I would think it should the other way around and this may have been a typo, but like this it does makes sense for the nested model in your example (Y ~ derived/source -> lakes are nested within source populations as they are replicates of colonization and evolution). I would think that I need one variable "lake" with eight levels that is nested within the "source" variable that has two levels only. The model would then be (coords ~ source/lakes). Does that make sense? How would I deal with the actual source populations? Simply assign them as their own source populations?

2.) I have to ask: given that the trajectory analysis is so straightforward, I would definitely prefer it over a potentially error-prone manual approach or not quantifying the angles at all. Is performing a TA with duplicated data a categorical no-go or can that be justified? I know that's a tricky question (how wrong is too wrong), but given that the PCAs with and without the duplicates appear almost identical I was wondering if this would be a justifiable workaround. Potentially in support of this, I did project the LS means onto the between-group PCA - as you suggested, thanks again! - (with a -hopefully sensible- model using lakes nested within source as described above) and if I draw vectors between derived lake populations and their sources it looks almost identical to the trajectory.analysis plot I got before with duplicated individuals.

I would be very grateful for your help.

Cheers,
Andi

messages.body_plain:
Virginia,

There are several issues here; primarily in the format of your TPS file.

First, you need to remove extraneous information after scale; specifically " PIXELS = 1 MM"  .  A simple ‘find/replace’ will let you do this in any text editor.  Once removed the file will read into geomorph correctly.

Then you need to ‘link up’ the classifier data with the specimens. This requires names in both files which are identical.  Your names are in the image names, but you need to remove some things, such as the path, and the ‘.gif’.  Also, note that in the TPS file images had a space in the names ‘APR 001’ while in the classifier they did not ‘APR001’.  These must be the same in both or you cannot link up the classifiers with the landmark data.

I did a quick fix of your file to read it in and reproduce the gpagen image you had. From this I suspect that orientation of your specimens under the camera was not the issue. Instead, I suspect that some specimens are flipped relative to others (righties and lefties).  This looks to be the case visually, and when I examine the maximal shape distance between specimens, it is enormous, and not biologically reasonable.

Hi everyone,

I am still quite new to morphometrics and I have done a couple of pilot studies investigating allometry effects of ear shape across populations and I greatly appreciate this thoughtful discussion across this thread. Being that I am new to morphometrics with no formal training, other than self-guided learning, I’m quite concerned that I too have been misinterpreting the results of these allometric / shape analyses. So I would like to ask the community if I am proceeding in the correct direction or if I should change my approach…

I’ve conducted a pilot study involving 2D data on ear shape for several different populations. My hypothesis is simply that ear shape differs by population. Here are some outputs I get from the Geomorph package in R.

My original interpretation of these results was that size alone had a significant effect on the shape of the ear but when population is also included, as a grouping factor, there was an interaction between size and shape for each population. These results suggest that each population has a different shape due to an interaction with allometry. Is this a fair interpretation of these results?

This is because my data separates out into parallel slopes (as is the case in the above figure); is this correct? I am currently planning to revisit this data but with the addition of another dimension (3D), and as I understand it, if I am on the right track I can essentially use the same approach but with the added dimension; is this correct? And if the parallel allometries appear again (which I anticipate they will since they are present in 2D) the interpretation would be the same.

Any insights would be helpful, thank you in advance for your time – Cheers.

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometric effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremy,

Your interpretation is close but not quite accurate.  You did not have a significant interaction between size and pop and the null hypothesis of parallel slopes is supported.  However, you have a significant pop effect, which means that at any given size, there is significant variation in shape among the pop levels.  Some would call this an “intercept test”, because as parallel lines never cross, it tests whether the points along the y-intercept differ.  But the intercept is a strange way to think of it, since there is not a case of no size.  A better way to think of it is that if you move along the size axis, some pop levels have consistently large PC scores and some have consistently lower PC scores, and the difference does not change as size changes.  (The PC scores change as size changes but the differences in PC scores stay the same.)

So, to summarize:
1) You have significant shape allometry.  Shape changes in a meaningful way as size increases, overall.
2) Each pop level has the same allometric pattern
3) However, at any size, there is variation in the different pop levels, meaning they differ in shape.  This shape difference persists along the size axis.

And for you understanding, a significant interaction would have revealed antiparallel allometries, meaning that shape changes in different ways with size for the different group levels.  In such cases, one cannot say “pop levels differ in shape”, as the need to qualify size would be important.  Because your allometries were parallel, it is easier to speak about shape differences without having to concern yourself with at which size you are speaking about shape differences.

Hope that helps!
Mike

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometric effect
messages.body_plain:
Jeremy,

1) All of your populations have the same relationship between shape and size (allometry).  There is no relationship between shape and allometry; that is like saying there is a relationship between shape and shape and size.  Allometry is the relationship.
2) Doing an analysis for shape differences without size, knowing that there is significant allometry, would be dangerous, because you run the risk of inferring shape differences as a result of size differences.  Simply do not do this.  Keep size as a covariate.
3) In the plot, if the lines appear close to each other, those populations do not differ much in shape at any given size.  If the lines are far apart, those populations differ more in shape at any given size.
4) Yes, whether an animal is small or large, the allometric pattern is the same.  You can somewhat predict how shape will change for a small animal in one population and know, compared to a large animal in a different population, if their shapes would be similar or not, based on the spacing of those lines.  This is why understanding the allometry is important.

Best,
Mike

> Jeremy,

> 1) All of your populations have the same relationship between shape and size (allometry).  There is no relationship between shape and allometry; that is like saying there is a relationship between shape and shape and size.  Allometry is the relationship.
> 2) Doing an analysis for shape differences without size, knowing that there is significant allometry, would be dangerous, because you run the risk of inferring shape differences as a result of size differences.  Simply do not do this.  Keep size as a covariate.
> 3) In the plot, if the lines appear close to each other, those populations do not differ much in shape at any given size.  If the lines are far apart, those populations differ more in shape at any given size.
> 4) Yes, whether an animal is small or large, the allometric pattern is the same.  You can somewhat predict how shape will change for a small animal in one population and know, compared to a large animal in a different population, if their shapes would be similar or not, based on the spacing of those lines.  This is why understanding the allometry is important.
>

Effectively if this is the case than regardless if one animal is exceptionally small and the other is exceptionally big, the shape of their ear is affected by allometry in the same way. > > > Hi Jeremy,
> > >
> > > Your interpretation is close but not quite accurate.  You did not have a significant interaction between size and pop and the null hypothesis of parallel slopes is supported.  However, you have a significant pop effect, which means that at any given size, there is significant variation in shape among the pop levels.  Some would call this an “intercept test”, because as parallel lines never cross, it tests whether the points along the y-intercept differ.  But the intercept is a strange way to think of it, since there is not a case of no size.  A better way to think of it is that if you move along the size axis, some pop levels have consistently large PC scores and some have consistently lower PC scores, and the difference does not change as size changes.  (The PC scores change as size changes but the differences in PC scores stay the same.)
> > >
> > > So, to summarize:
> > > 1) You have significant shape allometry.  Shape changes in a meaningful way as size increases, overall.
> > > 2) Each pop level has the same allometric pattern
> > > 3) However, at any size, there is variation in the different pop levels, meaning they differ in shape.  This shape difference persists along the size axis.
> > >

Hi Dean,
Thank you very much for the help!
I cleaned up my data and the matching specimen information. I tried to use left wings whenever possible but found 12 right wings. I removed them and got a new plot (attached). I also ran the maximal Procrustes distance and it went from 1.6436 to 1.6411.

These specimens while the same species are from a large range of places and have different wing lengths that I have already measured. I have a lot more wings to digitize so I'm trying to troubleshoot a little more.

On Thursday, July 6, 2017 at 3:52:14 PM UTC-4, Dean Adams wrote:

> Virginia,
>
>
> There are several issues here; primarily in the format of your TPS file.
>
>
>
> First, you need to remove extraneous information after scale; specifically " PIXELS = 1 MM"  .  A simple ‘find/replace’ will let you do this in any text editor.  Once removed the file will read into geomorph correctly.
>
>
>
> Then you need to ‘link up’ the classifier data with the specimens. This requires names in both files which are identical.  Your names are in the image names, but you need to remove some things, such as the path, and the ‘.gif’.  Also, note that in the TPS file images had a space in the names ‘APR 001’ while in the classifier they did not ‘APR001’.  These must be the same in both or you cannot link up the classifiers with the landmark data.
>
>
> I did a quick fix of your file to read it in and reproduce the gpagen image you had. From this I suspect that orientation of your specimens under the camera was not the issue. Instead, I suspect that some specimens are flipped relative to others (righties and lefties).  This looks to be the case visually, and when I examine the maximal shape distance between specimens, it is enormous, and not biologically reasonable.
>
>
> Another possibility is that you digitized some landmarks out of order; meaning that the homology of landmarks between specimens is not the same (landmark 4 is now thought to be landmark 5 for instance).
>
>
>
> I suggest you examine all of these digitizing issues, then try running things in the script below. After that, linking up the shape data with other variables can be accomplished using hints in the geomorph user guide:
>
>
>
> https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/raw/gh-pages/geomorph%20user%20guide/Quick_Guide_to_Geomorph-3.0.pdf

>
>

Virginia,

>From the PDistances I strongly suspect that you still have some left-right issues in the dataset.

Incidentally, if you can identify which are rights and you wish to flip them to be lefts, that is easy: just multiply one of the coordinates (x or y) by -1 for those specimens. An example below:

Mydata[,1,which(side=="r")] <- Mydata[,1,which(side=="r")]* -1  vv#reflect 'g'

This last line reflects the x-coordinates of all right-specimens to now be left-looking specimens, where:

Mydata = a 3D array of landmark coordinates for the specimens

Side =  a vector of R and L for each specimen

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Virginia,

A few other thoughts for identifying the rights and lefts.

First, one could try plotOutliers, which plots Procrustes distances from each specimen to the average. If only a few specimens are rights and the rest are lefts, the average should be closer to the lefts, and the few right-handed specimens will show up as the largest outliers.

Second, one could take the gpa-aligned specimens and plot them one at a time.  There you will be able to see which ones look ‘flipped’ relative to the others.

Generally, it is more cumbersome to identify these issue post-digitizing, but it is possible.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Hi all again

I have again been visiting this, for the Pst calculations, and I am wondering if I am on the right track in finding the within and among population morphological variation to then further calculate Pst. I did not use residuals, but rather had size as a co-variant.

This is what I have so far:

morph.data<-readland.tps("jminjaw.tps")
#read the landmarks back in (not a neccessary step, but I did it here because I had ran into trouble)
define.sliders(morph.data,nsliders=6)
#Defines the slider file - those files can be used multiple times, if the dataset is the same
sliders<-read.csv("curveslide.csv")
#Reads the slider file
cave.gpa<-gpagen(morph.data,curves=sliders)
#Runs a procrustes analysis
groups <- read.csv("ID-June.csv", header=TRUE, sep=";")
caves <- as.factor(groups$Cave)
#Reading in a crouping variable and getting the grouping into the right format
Datafr.gdf<-geomorph.data.frame(cave.gpa, caves=caves)
#Here the co-ordinates are made into a dataframe
procD.lm(coords~Csize,iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)
# Here the relationship between morphology and size are compared
procD.lm(coords~Csize+caves,iter=999, data=Datafr.gdf)
#here I test the differences among the caves with size as a covariant
Morph.dis<-morphol.disparity(coords~Csize, groups=NULL, data=Datafr.gdf, iter=999)
#Here I find the procrustes variance for the whole dataset, taking size into account
Morph.disgroups<-morphol.disparity(coords~Csize*caves, groups=~caves, data=Datafr.gdf, iter=999)
#Here I find the Procrustes variance for each cave and the distances among caves, taking size into account as co-variant

Regarding the heritability, then I have been reading up on that.

Here is a section from Mariani et al. 2012, which I have been looking at (Marine Ecology Progress Serise, 446:173-187),

"A commonly applied alternative is the phenotypic ‘analogue’ PST, which is simply estimated from the between population (VB) and within population (VW) phenotypic components of variation (Merilä 1997). PST has often been used interchangeably with QST (Merilä & Crnokrak 2001, Leinonen et al. 2008), typically assuming c = 1 and h2 = 0.5 (Saether et al. 2007), where c is the between-population additive genetic component and h2 is the within-population additive genetic component (‘narrow-sense herit - ability’). However, recently, Brommer (2011) argued that, especially in cases of diversifying selection, environmental and non-additive genetic components of phenotypic variation among populations are likely to be substantial and, probably, much greater than h2 (rather than much less as assumed when equating PST directly with QST). Therefore, Brommer (2011) suggested the alternative formulation: PST = cVB / (cVB + 2h2 VW) (1) Rather than specific values of c and h2 (which are generally unknown) it is their ratio which determines whether conclusions that QST (estimated as PST) de viates from the null hypothesis provided by FST may be appropriately conservative; low values (e.g. c/h2 < 0.2) suggest more robust conclusions (Brommer 2011). Therefore, we first generated overall and pairwise PST estimates, and secondly determined the minimum value of c/h2 required for each phenotypic trait to produce non-overlapping confidence limits between PST and FST."

I hope I am on the right track.

Bjarni

On Friday, March 24, 2017 at 8:59:51 AM UTC, bj...@mail.holar.is wrote:
> Thank you for this Ian!!!
>
> Will look these up and see where they take me.
>
> Bjarni
>
> On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 4:29:20 PM UTC, Ian Dworkin wrote:
> > Bjarni
> >
> >  More generally I would suggest digging into the fairly deep literature on Fst VS. Qst (even while using the approach for Pst mentioned by Mike and Dean).  There is a lot there but a few citations like
> >
> >  S. Hoban, J. L. Kelley, K. E. Lotterhos, M. F. Antolin, G. Bradburd, D. B. Lowry, M. L. Poss, L. K. Reed, A. Storfer, and M. C. Whitlock, “Finding the Genomic Basis of Local Adaptation: Pitfalls, Practical Solutions, and Future Directions.,” Am Nat, vol. 188, no. 4, pp. 379–397, Oct. 2016.
> >
> >  T. Leinonen, R. J. S. McCairns, R. B. O'Hara, and J. Merilä, “QST–FST comparisons: evolutionary and ecological insights from genomic heterogeneity,” Nature Reviews Genetics, vol. 14, no. 3, pp. 179–190, Feb. 2013.
> >
> > M. C. Whitlock, “Evolutionary inference from QST,” Mol Ecol, vol. 17, no. 8, pp. 1885–1896, 2008.
> >
> >
> > might be good places to start.
> >
> > On 23 March 2017 at 10:13, Adams, Dean [EEOBS] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > Bjarni,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I’ll add a few thoughts to what Mike suggested. First I will note though that the conundrum you are facing is directly analogous to the multivariate heritability issue faced some years ago in morphometrics, as I’ll explain below.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > For univariate data Pst is found as:  s^2_b / ( s^2_b + 2h^2 s^2_w)
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > where the s^2_b is the between population variance, s^2_w is the within population variance, and h^2 is the heritability.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > For the multivariate case, as Mike mentioned the variance components are now covariance matrices, and there are two obvious ways to obtain a scalar estimate of Pst. One way is to use take the trace of each of these first.  Here, one has the total SS between and the total SS within.  One can obtain these easily from a Procrustes anova.  Note then that one still requires an estimate of heritability, or without these one at least can use a range of possible values.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > The alternative is to retain these as covariance matrices, perform the matrix computations, and then obtain the trace of the outcome. Like Mike I do not know if this will arrive at the same numerical value, but based on the multivariate heritability discussion some years ago, my suspicion is that they will not.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Now, the description of methods above is precisely that used in multivariate heritability back in the early 2000s. Monteiro and colleagues proposed using summed Procrustes distances to obtain SS, analogous to the Procrustes anova description above. Alternatively, Klingenberg proposed a full matrix approach, much like Mike and I mentioned (note: their joint paper in 2005 in Syst. Biol. describes the different perspectives and interpretations).  Some colleagues and I used both of these approaches in a 2006 empirical paper to compare them, and while estimates gave similar biological conclusions, there was more to be gained from the full multivariate approach in terms of understanding patterns of shape variation.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > So given that discussion on multivariate heritability, I agree with Mike and am inclined to suggest you retain things using full multivariate covariance matrices until the end of the procedure. That requires obtaining the between- and within-group covariance matrices from the manova SSCP, and using these for Pst estimates. The one complication that remains then is the heritability estimate. To generalize the Pst equation above, it seems that this would be represented as a p x p diagonal matrix, with the h^2 found on the diagonal.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > One final comment, I know of a paper that compared Fst and Pst where the latter were obtained from GM shape data (Leinonen et al 2006). However, they found Pst for the first PC and second PC of shape univariately, so I would not recommend their approach.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Leinonen, et. al. 2006. Contrasting patterns of body shape and neutral genetic divergence in marine and lake populations of threespine sticklebacks. J. Evol. Biol. 19: 1803–1812.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Good luck,
> > >
> > >
> > > Dean
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Dr. Dean C. Adams
> > >
> > > Professor
> > >
> > > Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology
> > >

> > > From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com [mailto:geomorph-...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Mike Collyer
> > > Sent: Thursday, March 23, 2017 8:04 AM
> > > To: bj...@mail.holar.is
> > > Cc: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
> > > Subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Pst calculations
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Bjarni,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > This is a question I am less likely to give a good answer, as I do not fundamentally work in quantitative genetics or population genetics, but I’ll offer two routes to consider and let somebody else chime in if there is an ardent preference.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Procrustes variance is the sum of squared distances of observations from the mean, divided by degrees of freedom, irrespective of the number of dimensions of the tangent space.It can also be described as the trace of either a p x p covariance matrix or an n x n covariance matrix, where the former is found from the cross-products of variables and the latter from crossproducts of observations.  Either way, the trace is the same.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > The reason these alternative explanations is important is because how does one generalize the concept of Fst, Qst, or Pst for multivariate data?  Let’s use Qst for simplicity.  Qst = varB/(varB + 2*varW), where B and W represent between- and within-population additive genetic notation of variances.  If we use the trace of matrices B and W for covariance matrices to get Procrustes variances and there is only one variable, then the trace of the 1 x 1 covariance matrices is the variance for the single variable.  Thus, we arrive at the same answer.  Alternatively, if we calculate the matrix product (B + 2*W)^1 x B and take the trace of this covariance matrix product, which is a generalization of the formula, and if we have only one variable, then again, we get the same answer.  These are two generalizations that work for a single variable.  They also produce the same answer for multivariate data, as long as n degrees of freedom are used (where n is the number of observations).  I believe in Qst measurements, n is used for degrees of freedom in all cases.  If this is not the case, then the two generalizations might produce different answers.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > I’m not sure if the two generalizations produce the same answer for Pst.  You might have to verify that, but if they don’t, I’m more inclined to favor the latter generalization (matrix product before trace), just because it is consistent with other statistical approaches.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Again, this is not in my wheelhouse, so somebody can probably shed better light on this than me.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > In geomorph, you can use residuals and fitted values from procD.lm or advanced.procD.lm to construct matrix products or feed them into morphol.disparity with the equation, e.g.,
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > residuals ~ 1
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > which returns the Procrustes variance across all n values.  This should allow you to make these estimates.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Cheers!
> > >
> > > Mike

The first PC, as a surrogate for shape, can miss important components of inter-specimen variation.  More importantly, if the first PC axis does not align well with population structure, you run the risk of making improper inferences.  For example, let’s say that the first PC just happens to be most associated with allometric variation in shape and the second PC with subpopulation variation.  If you use use first PC scores only, you miss the appropriate characterization of the population structure in your estimates.

messages.body_plain:
Avi,

If you have a model like this, Y ~ A/B/C, you can use nested.update twice to adjust the F values.

For example,

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/B/C, …)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~B/C)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~A/B)
summary(fit)

I’m not sure what you mean by using the middle factor twice, but I suppose it is possible to have a model like, Y ~ A/C + B/C.  If that is the case, then the protocol would be,

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/C + B/C, …)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~B/C)
fit <- nested.update(fit, ~A/C)
summary(fit)

Hope that helps,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Nested MANOVA with 3 factors
messages.body_plain:
Avi,

You might have to make your original fit as

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/B + B/C)

When R encounters a formula as Y ~A/B, it expands it to Y ~ A + A/B.  Writing it as Y ~ A/B is just a short-cut.  I suggested the Y ~A/B/C approach, but I did not consider how it might be expanded, internally.  Apparently it did not include B as fixed effect in reference to C.

If you have further trouble, you might consider

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A + B + A/B + B/C)

And if neither or these do not work, then I’m afraid you have run into a limitation for what the nested.update function can do.  We would like to make this function more universal, ideally, but it’s not an easy one to program for all situations.

Hopefully one of those solutions works.

Mike

messages.subject: Fluctuating asymmetry with individual covariates
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph list:

I am assessing shape variation in damselflies wings that live in oligotrophic and eutrophic lakes and one of my goals is to evaluate fluctuating asymmetry as a proxy of the individuals' condition and environmental stress they suffer.

Using bilat.symmetry function separately for the two populations, I have found that individuals of both lakes possess directional and fluctuating asymmetry in the anterior wings but the posterior wings are asymmetric only in the eutrophic lake. I would like to include the levels of ectoparasitism (number aquatic mites each individual carry) to see if it is related with the degree of asymmetry damselflies show. Since bilat.symmetry function does not have an argument to include continuous variables I was wondering how to proceed.

I have read in the great geomorph manual that you can extract the asymmetric components of shape and that they can be used in subsequent analyses, but I would be very grateful if someone could advise me how to do it.

a) Can I perform a MANCOVA in R using the asymmetric components of shape of both populations as a response variable having as predictors: a categorical (population origin) and a continuous variable (number of parasites)?

b) If that is the case, should I pool the individuals of both populations before the bilat.symmetry analysis or I would merge the asymmetric components of shape that are the result of two separate analyses for each population?

b) Do I have to correct the degrees of freedom for these analyses?

Thanks for your help,

Roberto Munguía-Steyer

messages.subject: Sample size and effect sizes compare.pls
messages.subject_clean: Sample size and effect sizes compare.pls
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I'm trying to use the compare.pls function to compare the strength of integration of traits between three different species. For two of these species (HC & DE), my sample size is around 30 individuals, and for the third (HV), over 100 individuals. I am aware that, according to "On the comparison of the strength of morphological integration across morphometric datasets", the use of Rpls values is dependant on sample size, so I am using the recommended compare.pls function to compare the strength of integration between these three species. However, I want to make sure I'm interpreting the compare.pls output correctly because these results (in particular the effect sizes) also seem to depend on the sample size.

If I run compare.pls with the 3 full datasets, then we get effect sizes (the $sample.z object) of:

HV    3.334794          DE 1.365760          HC  1.930840

If, however, I run compare.pls for HC & DE plus reduced dataset with a random sample of 30 rows from HV, then the effect size for HV is very different.

HVRed 0.8437519                  DE 1.3657602       HC 1.9308398

So this effect size is apparently dependent on sample size. Is that as it should be? I think I may have misunderstood from the paper what exactly this effect size is, and whether it should or should not vary with sample size. Is it rather the $pairwise.z object that is less affected by sample size? For what it's worth, this doesn't change the inference based on p-values in the compare.pls output.

My data are attached. The code I used was:
#
DEint<-integration.test(A=DE,partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=c(rep("adv",7),rep("agg",7)),iter=1000,seed=NULL)
HCint<-integration.test(A=HC,partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=c(rep("adv",8),rep("agg",8)),iter=1000,seed=NULL)
HVint<-integration.test(A=HV,partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=c(rep("adv",5),rep("agg",6)),iter=1000,seed=NULL)
HVReducedint<-integration.test(A=HVRed,partition.gp <http://partition.gp>=c(rep("adv",5),rep("agg",6)),iter=1000,seed=NULL)

fullcompare<-compare.pls(DEint,HCint,HVint)
Reducedcompare<-compare.pls(DEint,HCint,HVReducedint)
#

Note that these are phenotypic traits but not morphological landmarks, and that I measured a few different traits for each species (but these traits still fall into the two proposed modules).

Thanks for any advice!

Michael Reichert

messages.body_plain:
Roberto,

It is best to pool the samples prior to the bilat.asymmetry analysis, as this function also performs the Procrustes superimposition, which should be done on all specimens simultaneously.

Once that is completed you can output the asymmetric shape components for further analysis; say, comparing the degree of asymmetry in different levels of ectoparasitism, etc.

As for df and MANCOVA, if the above analysis is performed using procD.lm, this is a permutation-based MANCOVA, so that is much less of an issue. For parametric assessment of significance, df matter a great deal, but that is not what is implemented in geomorph.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Derek,

The pc.summary is a list of multiple objects, the same as one would find with prcomp.  The only way to make it data frame coercible is to isolate part of that list that is also data frame coercible.  For example:

myPCA$pc.summary <- myPCA$pc.summary$importance # this is the table of percent explained for eigenvectors
write.xlsx(myPCA$pc.summary, “filename and path”)

Or you can simply write some of the subcomponents

write.xlsx(myPCA$pc.summary$importance, “filename and path”)
write.xlsx(myPCA$pc.summary$rotation, “another filename and path”)
write.xlsx(myPCA$pc.summary$x, “yet another filename and path”)

And if you are interested in just what you can pull out,

attributes(myPCA$pc.summary)

will list all objects.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,
I tried both:

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/B + B/C)

fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A + B + A/B + B/C)

and they both worked! giving the exact same results after nested.update.
So I guess I shouldn't worry about choosing only one of them.
But generally speaking, can I extend this to many more nested factors (3/4/5) like this:
fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/B + B/C + C/D + D/E)
or
fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A + B + C + D + A/B + B/C + C/D + D/E)

Am I right?

Thanks a lot,
Avi

On Tuesday, July 11, 2017 at 8:05:21 PM UTC+3, Michael Collyer wrote:

> Avi,
>
> You might have to make your original fit as
>
> fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A/B + B/C)
>
> When R encounters a formula as Y ~A/B, it expands it to Y ~ A + A/B.  Writing it as Y ~ A/B is just a short-cut.  I suggested the Y ~A/B/C approach, but I did not consider how it might be expanded, internally.  Apparently it did not include B as fixed effect in reference to C.
>
> If you have further trouble, you might consider
>
> fit <- procD.lm(Y ~ A + B + A/B + B/C)
>
> And if neither or these do not work, then I’m afraid you have run into a limitation for what the nested.update function can do.  We would like to make this function more universal, ideally, but it’s not an easy one to program for all situations.
>
> Hopefully one of those solutions works.
>
> Mike

> > > summary(fit)
> > >

anteriores_sim$asymm.shape

Roberto

messages.subject: advanced.ProcD.lm with 3 predictors and interactions
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm analyzing data from an experiment in which individuals from different sites were run through an experimental test (each at their home site). Individuals either failed or succeeded at the challenge. I'm interested in whether body shape contributes to success in this challenge, after controlling for the effects of centroid size and site of origin.

I'm wondering how to include interactions between these three predictors, and how to test for their effects using the advanced.procD.lm framework. I think that all possible interactions might reasonably be hypothesized to have an effect on body shape as described below.

size - allometry
site - mean population differences
success - functional effect of body shape on success
size:site - allometric trajectory differs by population
size:success - success depends on allometric component of shape
site:success - success depends on site-based differences in shape
size:site:success - success depends on site-based differences in the allometric trajectory of shape.

Following Collyer et al 2015 (A method for analysis of phenotypic change for phenotypes described by high-dimensional data) and these helpful blog posts <https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/wiki/advanced.procD.lm-for-pairwise-tests-and-model-comparisons> I tried to start with the full model and then iteratively test against a reduced model by pulling out one interaction term at a time. Then, when I only had terms that were significant I would have to consider adding ~groups and ~slope terms.

On my first iteration the 3-way interaction did not significantly improve model fit so I dropped it. How do I decide which two-way interaction to test next? If one (for example, site:success) is significant, do I try to test/drop the others or do I stop there? I think I'm ultimately interested in the LS means of the different levels of site:success. The LS means output differ depending on which other predictors are included in the model and I'm unsure how to determine which set of predictors is appropriate to include.

Thanks for your help and consideration.

Best,
Ben

PhD Candidate - Palkovacs Lab
Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
University of California at Santa Cruz
Long Marine Lab

Santa Cruz, CA 95060

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I'm trying to compare mean shape of specimens who belong to different groups (e.g. female, sites). I'd like to use plotRefToTarget for this, but the function mshape in the guide only specify how to compare mean shape of "Y.gpa$coords" (which mean all specimens) to a specific specimen. I searched the help for mshape and couldn't find any argument like "groups =", so I guess the solution should lie in creating a sub-group of $coords. I thought of using 'subset' on gdf since I already have coords and factors all together, but they're not in the same matrix. Is there a way to use gdf$shape or Y.gpa$coords with my classifiers.csv (already included in both Y.gpa$coords & gdf$shape) to extract only specific rows (e.g. time== "before")?
When trying this:
A = subset(gdf$shape, time == "before")
I get:
Error in time == "before" :
  comparison (1) is possible only for atomic and list types
Avi

messages.body_plain:
Dana,

This error is a base R error but what is causing it to happen is not clear. The only thing that jumps out as a possible explanation is that the design matrix you are attempting to create is rather ridiculous. The number of parameters needed for all two-way, three-way, four-way, five-way, and six-way interactions should be so numerous to believe that there are no redundancies. Climate and population looks to be suspicious. I doubt you populations experience all levels of climate. So why have them interact?  Haplotypes and genotypes are two others where variable interactions make little sense.

Although we try to anticipate problems with this function, some - like the analysis you are attempting - are not easy to anticipate. We could try to get to the heart of the analytical issue, but I am pretty sure it will be because of your illogical model design. In this case, I think a better question to explore is why you want to have all of these variable interactions?  It simply does not make much sense from a model design perspective.

In summary, I think your illogical variable interactions led to a model design matrix that could not be decomposed via QR decomposition or had no rank or something like this. The R error basically says, "An attempt to summarize something that contained nothing failed."

My guess is because of those illogical interactions creating many columns of nothingness in your design matrix.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Emma is correct. You are making this far more difficult than it needs to be, and your pipeline of going in and out of R is very prone to error (both I/O and user-based). A few comments on what should be done in geomorph:

First, all specimens should be subjected to a single GPA, not separate ones (as your post implied). Otherwise, the data are in incommensurate rotations in shape space.

Second, finding the mean shape for each group may be accomplished in myriad ways in R.  Some are more ‘blunt stick’ approaches while others are more statistically elegant. Some simple examples include using mshape() on each set of aligned specimens, and some sort of loop or tapply function.  The more general and elegant approach is to use a linear function of shape ~ groups and extract the means. This is done as:

means <- aggregate(two.d.array(Y.gpa$coords) ~ group, FUN=mean)

where Y.gpa$coords is the GPA-aligned shape data and group is the vector designating to which group each specimen belongs. Here the function two.d.array() is used to turn the 3D array into a 2D matrix.  Then, if one wishes to ‘put it back’ into a 3D array, the arrayspecs() function will do this.

Again I note that all of this is described in the geomorph manual, and does not require going in and out of R, which is prone to errors.

Dean

Dean, thank you for your reply. I apologize for not being as clear as I hoped to be in my first two posts. To clarify, I have 6 sets of data based on 6 different shapes. Each data set contains landmark coordinates for around 300 specimens (some vary slightly), representing ~10 specimens each for 31 species. I ran a GPA on each shape separately because I figured running it as a single dataset would be prone to errors since the TPS input files are separate and the scale bars are unique for each.

Are you saying it's possible, even preferable, to combine these into a single TPS and input it into R, thus creating a combined set of landmark coordinates for all 6 shapes? Then, I would run a GPA analysis on all simultaneously? If so, is there an elegant way to calculate means for the 6 shape sets within the data block? I have already previously followed your guide to calculate means within R for the 6 shapes separately, using the same "aggregate" suggestion you included in your post here. I only use the export-to-Excel function to keep track of all of the results from all analyses I'm performing.

I sincerely appreciate your assistance.

> First, all specimens should be subjected to a single GPA, not separate ones (as your post implied). Otherwise, the data are in incommensurate rotations in shape space.

>

>
>
>
> means <- aggregate(two.d.array(Y.gpa$coords) ~ group, FUN=mean)
>
>
>
> where Y.gpa$coords is the GPA-aligned shape data and group is the vector designating to which group each specimen belongs. Here the function two.d.array() is used to turn the 3D array into a 2D matrix.  Then, if one wishes to ‘put it back’ into a 3D array, the arrayspecs() function will do this.

messages.body_plain:
If the six landmark configurations are the same (same number of landmarks in same dimensions), one can combine landmarks easily as follows:

LM.all <- array(c(LM1, LM2, LM3, LM4, LM5, LM6), c(p, k, n))

where p is the number of landmarks, k is the number of dimensions, and n is the number of specimens, equal to n1 + n2 + n3 + n4 + n5 + n6, and LMi refers to the landmarks of set i.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
GPA has to be performed on the same number of landmarks (and plethspecies$land has the same number for each specimen).

You can run GPA on each “shape”, use coords.subset + mshape to get means (see coords.subset example), and then use combine.subsets, provided the means are in the same order, to concatenate the six shapes into one set.  This function can also scale the six shapes to be proportional in size, in case one shape is small and another is large, for example.  Then when you use compare.multi.evol.rates, you just have to be careful to make sure that the 6 landmark number designations are accurate.

One caveat, you should also get mean centroid sizes to use in combine.subsets, if you want to appropriately scale configurations.  As you are going from 10 shapes each to 1 per species, the typical workflow is different than if you are working at the individual level.  (In that case, combine.subsets would be easier, as it can perform GPA.  That is not an option for you.)  Hopefully the help files are each helpful to point you in the right direction.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Derek,

The function compare.multi.evol.rates() is used to compare the rate of one multi-dimensional trait against another multi-dimensional trait (or more of them).  Thus, one either has multiple traits to compare “the rate of evolution in arm variation versus leg variation” or one compares the rates of evolution in subsets of landmarks from within the same shape or landmark configuration.

The example was for a case of the latter. Here, the entire head was a shape, and the groups of landmarks designated two components: the cranium and the mandible, for which rates were quantified and compared.  Mike’s comment on cords.subset() function was for how to deal with means for such traits if these are desired: which they would be in your case since you have multiple individuals per species and thus require the mean for each species for the subsequent rate analysis.

Alternatively, if one had two different shape components (e.g., heads and arms), these would be aligned separately, the means for each species found separately, and then the rate comparison would be performed.

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Okay, but in your case you have six separate landmark configurations digitized - separately - on 10 specimens each for 31 species, correct?  For the salamander heads, one needs to merely assign a landmark to a subset, as they are all in the same configuration.  As Dean hinted, if he wanted to add salamander tails and took separate photos of tails, he would have separate data sets but the function assumes there is one.  So you have to trick the function.  You can do this with combine.subsets.  You just then have to make a grouping variable that matches the numbers and sequences according to the way you combined them.

Mike

> Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethspecies$land) #GPA-alignment
> land.gp <http://land.gp/><-c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B") #mandible and cranium subsets
> EMR<-compare.multi.evol.rates(A=Y.gpa$coords,gp=land.gp <http://land.gp/>, Subset=TRUE, phy= plethspecies$phy,iter=999)"

This function can also scale the six shapes to be proportional in size, in case one shape is small and another is large, for example.  Then when you use compare.multi.evol.rates, you just have to be careful to make sure that the 6 landmark number designations are accurate.
> >
> > One caveat, you should also get mean centroid sizes to use in combine.subsets, if you want to appropriately scale configurations.  As you are going from 10 shapes each to 1 per species, the typical workflow is different than if you are working at the individual level. I should add that this is one way to do it.  The other is to make the 3D arrays into 2D matrices and concatenate the different matrices, and use Subset = FALSE as an argument.  You can do this with two.d.array() followed by the cbind function (binding matrices by columns).  The way I previously recommended was to turn multiple shapes into one large configuration (with each potentially scaled to relative size); this other way keeps the shapes separate but does not allow scaling to relative size.  I’m not sure that the relative size matters for estimating evolutionary rates.

Regardless, you have to concatenate data and getting back to your original premise, doing it outside of R is unneeded and perhaps error inducing.

Mike

messages.subject: Digital morphology data survey: ethics on data generation & use
messages.subject_clean: Digital morphology data survey: ethics on data generation & use
messages.body_plain:
Dear Geomorph Users,

I kindly ask your help in completing a short survey on trends in digital morphology data generation and use as part of a perspectives piece on the “Ethics of data sharing in the age of digital imaging”, which I will present at this year’s BioSyst EU meeting in Gothenburg, Sweden (http://www.conferencemanager.se/BiosystEU2017/speakers-and-symposia.html).

We are aware that many recommendations have been made lately on best practices in this field, however we as a community are still far from a consensus on how our data should be managed - both from the perspective of the people generating it and the people requesting it.

Your responses are anonymous, and I will post the results here at the end. The questions are focused on 3D digital morphology data (CT, laser scanning, etc), but please feel free to answer if you also deal with 2D images.

To go to the survey, click here: https://goo.gl/forms/3owPtxSLzDs6WjqC3

The site will remain active for the next 2 weeks, until Friday, 11 August.

Almost every question has an “Other” option where you can enter text, so please give as much information and opinions as possible so we can accurately represent your concerns.

Thank you for your time!

Christy Hipsley & Emma Sherratt

Mike, I cracked it! Your assistance was particularly instrumental - many, many thanks!. I've only done it with 2 shapes so far, but combining the other 4 with them should be a snap now. Basically, I ran a GPA on each shape again, calculated the means using the aggregate function as I did previously, converted each of those results to 2D arrays, combined both of these arrays, converted the combo array back into 3D, and then called it in to the multivariate evolutionary rate function. Not too bad once the pathway has been deciphered.

Initially, though, I received the error "Error in C[rownames(x), rownames(x)] : subscript out of bounds" and found a previous thread that you and Emma assisted with: https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph/issues/10

I had a hunch my names were not matching either (in my tree and combined data array), but I was unable to get the match function to do much for me and I'm wondering I am just using it wrong. I used it with my data, but to bring it back to an earlier example, I tried it with the plethspecies dataset and got the same result as with mine. I set it up like:

match(plethspecies$land, plethspecies$phy, nomatch = NA_integer_, incomparables = NULL)

and it returns a series of "NA". I may not need this function again for this current task, but my curiosity is piqued.

> > > > > > > > > Emma is correct. You are making this far more difficult than it needs to be, and your pipeline of going in and out of R is very prone to error (both I/O and user-based). A few comments on what should be done in geomorph:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > First, all specimens should be subjected to a single GPA, not separate ones (as your post implied). Otherwise, the data are in incommensurate rotations in shape space.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Second, finding the mean shape for each group may be accomplished in myriad ways in R.  Some are more ‘blunt stick’ approaches while others are more statistically elegant. Some simple examples include using mshape() on each set of aligned specimens, and some sort of loop or tapply function.  The more general and elegant approach is to use a linear function of shape ~ groups and extract the means. This is done as:
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > means <- aggregate(two.d.array(Y.gpa$coords) ~ group, FUN=mean)
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > where Y.gpa$coords is the GPA-aligned shape data and group is the vector designating to which group each specimen belongs. Here the function two.d.array() is used to turn the 3D array into a 2D matrix.  Then, if one wishes to ‘put it back’ into a 3D array, the arrayspecs() function will do this.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Again I note that all of this is described in the geomorph manual, and does not require going in and out of R, which is prone to errors.
